newsitem.title: CHINA: North Korea defector passes birthday amid warnings.
newsitem.headline: North Korea defector passes birthday amid warnings.

text.p: The most senior leader ever to defect from North Korea passed his 74th birthday behind a police cordon in Beijing on Monday as former comrades outside demanded his return and issued harsh warnings to arch-rival Seoul.

Hwang Jang-yop, a top adviser to North Korea's supreme leader Kim Jong-il, began his sixth day as the focus of an international diplomatic crisis centred on the South Korean mission in Beijing where he sought refuge on Wednesday.

North Korean officials keeping vigil outside the Chinese police cordon around the mission accused South Korea of abducting Hwang and issued dour warnings of the consequences of any attempt to move him out of Beijing to the South.
"If they make him go to Seoul, I think there will be war," said one official who declined to be identified.
"They kidnapped him... that is a very bad thing," he said. "We want him back."
Pyongyang officials who have watched outside the South Korean mission since last week have threatened to use force to block any attempt to take Hwang to Seoul.
China, an unwilling participant in the diplomatic crisis between the two hostile ends of the Korean peninsula, has appealed to both sides to act calmly to resolve the affair.

The United States has urged Pyongyang to avoid all provocative actions and has said it is closely monitoring developments after an assassination attempt against a former North Korean defector near Seoul on Saturday night.
South Korea accused Pyongyang agents of shooting 32-year-old defector Li Il-nam in an attack that left him critically ill with a bullet still lodged in his skull.

Analysts say the North has suffered huge loss of face over the defection of Hwang, who was ranked 24th in the hierarchy of his Stalinist homeland and was the architect of its governing ideology of Juche, or strict self-reliance.

The most senior defection from North Korea comes as the communist hermit nation struggles to cope with an imploding economy and widespread food shortages caused by two years of flood disasters and failed harvests.
The crisis cast a pall over Pyongyang's celebrations to mark Kim Jong-il's 55th birthday on Sunday, with analysts finding little trace of a festive mood in the state-sponsored partying.
North and South Korea have been arch-enemies since the 1950-53 Korean civil war ended only in a truce.
South Korean officials have said Hwang is spending his time reading and sleeping at the mission but have given no details on how he would mark his birthday.

After a request for tighter security from Seoul, Chinese paramilitary and regular police have posted a heavy guard around the mission and have stationed a large crowd control truck armed with water cannon and a bullet-proof car outside its doors.

Officers prepared bands of anti-tyre spikes to be laid across the quiet tree-lined streets of the diplomatic quarter and turned away scores of would-be Chinese travellers seeking visas at the South Korean consular offices in the mission.

"It took two days on the train to get here...but the office is closed," said one ethnic-Korean visa-seeker from the northeastern Chinese province of Heilongjiang who had hoped to complete the formalities needed to marry a South Korean man.
"We don't know when the office will open again, they haven't told us anything," she said.
